screens.title: Encapsulation and Access Specifiers
screens.narratorSegment: In this chapter you will learn why encapsulation is central to maintainable game code and how C++ access specifiers work together with Unreal Engine's reflection macros to create safe, designer-friendly classes. Encapsulation bundles data and the functions that operate on it, protecting an object's internal state from accidental changes while making clear, stable interfaces for other code and designers. You will see concrete C++ examples that use public, protected, and private to set visibility and then learn how UPROPERTY and UFUNCTION specifiers control editor editability and Blueprint exposure. We'll step through a working AMyDoor actor: how private state is visible but not editable, how editable settings are exposed to designers, and how BlueprintCallable and BlueprintPure functions are chosen. You will also practice common patterns: prefer private state, expose state through controlled functions, and favor read-only exposure to Blueprints unless writing must be allowed. By the end you'll know what to expose, what to protect, and how to keep debugging manageable when teams mix C++ and Blueprints. What small change will make your next actor safer to use in a level?

screens.title: What is encapsulation?
screens.narratorSegment: Encapsulation is an OOP principle that bundles an object's data and the methods that operate on it, while restricting direct external access to those internals. In a game, encapsulation means you expose a clear, small public interface—actions and queries designers or other systems may call—while keeping the actual state and helper functions private. A practical example from this chapter is a door actor: we keep bIsOpen private and provide OpenDoor and CloseDoor functions. That way, any rules about invulnerability frames, locking, or network replication live in the functions, not scattered across Blueprints or other actors. A common misconception is that visibility is only about hiding variables; in practice it is about preserving invariants. If you let every system write to health or position, you lose the ability to enforce game rules consistently. Encapsulation makes refactoring safe: you can change the implementation details—how the door interpolates or what internal timers it uses—without changing its public contract. Your takeaway is simple: expose behavior, not implementation. Ask yourself when adding a variable: does external code really need to set this, or should it call a method that enforces rules?

keyIdea.title: Encapsulation defined
keyIdea.text: Expose a minimal public interface; keep internal state private so rules live in methods, not in scattered code.

content.html:
Core Concept › Encapsulation
What is encapsulation?
Bundle data and methods; protect internal state and expose controlled behavior.
Definition & metaphor
Think of a car: the steering wheel, accelerator and brakes are the interface you use. You do not tinker with the engine's gears directly. Encapsulation does the same for classes.
  • Protects internal state from accidental modification.
  • Makes interfaces stable and predictable.
  • Enables refactoring without breaking users.
Concrete example
// In a player class
private:
    float PlayerStamina; // protected by encapsulation
public:
    void SpendStamina(float Amount); // only this enforces rules
    float GetStamina() const; // safe read
Designers set initial stamina via EditAnywhere; only C++ functions change it during gameplay.
Analogy
Interface is what you touch; implementation stays hidden.
Common mistake
Making everything public or writable from Blueprints leads to unpredictable state changes.
Key takeaway
Expose behavior, not raw state.

screens.title: public, protected, private in C++
screens.narratorSegment: C++ provides three basic access specifiers: public, protected, and private. Public members form the class's external interface and can be accessed from any code; use them for actions and queries you intend other systems to call. Protected members are available to the class and its subclasses; they are useful when you expect derived classes to extend behavior but do not want general code to modify internals. Private members are accessible only inside the class itself and are the safest place to store core state. A concrete example is a player or door: keep CurrentHealth or bIsOpen private so only controlled functions can mutate them. A typical misconception is treating protected as a free-for-all for subclasses; prefer protected sparingly and provide protected accessors rather than exposing raw fields. When in doubt, default to private and open the minimal interface needed. This discipline helps teams because fixing a rule in one central function propagates everywhere, while scattered writes from various places make reasoning and debugging much harder. Which members in your current class truly need to be public? public, protected, private in C++ means public = external api, protected = for subclasses, private = internal core; default to private and open minimally.. In practical terms, which members should be accessible and to whom. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Access Specifiers
public vs protected vs private
Decide who can read and write class members.
public
Accessible anywhere. Use for methods that form your API: actions and queries that other systems should call.
public:
    void OpenDoor();
    bool IsDoorOpen() const;
protected
Accessible to the class and derived classes. Use sparingly for extension points, not as general writable state.
protected:
    float DoorOpenDuration; // subclasses may tweak timing
private
Accessible only inside the class. Store core invariants here so only controlled functions can change them.
private:
    bool bIsOpen; // only mutated via OpenDoor/CloseDoor
    float CurrentOpenAlpha;
Common mistake
Making everything public for convenience creates fragile codebases where any module can break class invariants.
Pro tip
Default to private; add public getters or actions that validate inputs and enforce rules.

screens.title: UPROPERTY() — Editor visibility and Blueprint access
screens.narratorSegment: Unreal's UPROPERTY macro sits on top of C++ access control and tells the Editor and Blueprint system how to surface a member. EditAnywhere makes a property editable in the Details panel for instances and placed actors; use it for tunable settings designers should change at edit time. VisibleAnywhere shows runtime values but prevents editing, which is perfect for showing current internal state without letting designers accidentally overwrite it. BlueprintReadWrite allows Blueprints to both read and set a property, which is convenient but risky for internal state; prefer BlueprintReadOnly when Blueprints only need to observe a value, and use BlueprintCallable functions to mutate state under controlled rules. Category groups properties in the Details panel, improving discoverability for non-programmers. A concrete header example in the chapter shows bIsOpen as VisibleAnywhere and OpenSpeed as EditAnywhere with BlueprintReadWrite. Consider the trade-off: VisibleAnywhere + private C++ access means designers can see a runtime flag but only C++ code can change it. This separation is exactly why UPROPERTY complements C++ encapsulation: one controls code-level visibility, the other controls editor and Blueprint exposure. Which properties in your actors should designers see but never edit during runtime?

keyIdea.title: UPROPERTY roles
keyIdea.text: UPROPERTY controls Editor and Blueprint exposure while C++ access specifiers control code visibility; use them together to protect state and enable tuning.

content.html:
UPROPERTY()
Control Editor visibility and Blueprint access
Match C++ encapsulation with Editor exposure.
Common specifiers
  • EditAnywhere: editable in the Details panel for instances.
  • VisibleAnywhere: visible but not editable; good for runtime diagnostics.
  • BlueprintReadWrite: Blueprints can read and write the property.
  • BlueprintReadOnly: Blueprints can only read the property.
  • Category: organizes properties in the Details panel.
Header example
// MyDoor.h
private:
    UPROPERTY(VisibleAnywhere, Category = "Door State")
    bool bIsOpen;

    UPROPERTY(EditAnywhere, BlueprintReadWrite, Category = "Door Settings")
    float OpenSpeed;
bIsOpen is visible but only C++ changes it. OpenSpeed is editable and accessible to Blueprints for tuning.
When to use EditAnywhere
For values designers should tune per-instance in the level.
When to use VisibleAnywhere
To expose runtime state without allowing edits from the Editor.
Pitfall
Using BlueprintReadWrite for internal state opens mutation from many places—prefer functions instead.

screens.title: UFUNCTION() — Exposing behavior to Blueprints
screens.narratorSegment: UFUNCTION determines how C++ functions appear in Blueprints and how they behave in the graph. BlueprintCallable exposes a function as a standard executable node with execution pins; use it for actions that change state, trigger effects, or perform work. BlueprintPure exposes a function as a read-only node without execution pins; these functions should be const, have no side effects, and return the same output for the same inputs — ideal for getters or deterministic calculations. BlueprintImplementableEvent declares a function that Blueprints implement; the C++ side only declares the contract. BlueprintNativeEvent allows both a C++ implementation and an override in Blueprint, with C++ serving as the fallback. A concrete example: ToggleDoor as BlueprintCallable to change bIsOpen, and IsDoorOpen as BlueprintPure to query state. A common misconception is using pure for convenience when the method actually modifies state. That breaks the Blueprint graph's expectation of purity and can create subtle bugs. When designing your A P I, pick the specifier that matches the function's behavioral contract, not how you want to wire Blueprint nodes. UFUNCTION() — Exposing behavior to Blueprints means blueprintcallable for actions with side effects, blueprintpure for const, deterministic queries; implementable/native events for blueprint-driven logic.. In practical terms, choosing blueprintcallable, blueprintpure, and event types correctly. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
UFUNCTION()
Expose functions to Blueprints
Match node behavior to function behavior.
BlueprintCallable
Use for actions that change state or have side effects — they appear with execution pins in Blueprint graphs.
UFUNCTION(BlueprintCallable, Category = "Door Actions")
void ToggleDoor();
BlueprintPure / Events
Pure functions are const, with no side effects. ImplementableEvent and NativeEvent let Blueprints supply behavior or override C++ fallback implementations.
UFUNCTION(BlueprintPure, Category = "Door State")
bool IsDoorOpen() const;

UFUNCTION(BlueprintImplementableEvent)
void OnDoorOpened();
Example
Make OpenDoor BlueprintCallable so level Blueprints can trigger it safely.
Misuse
Marking side-effecting functions as pure will confuse Blueprints and break assumptions about execution order.
Takeaway
Choose specifiers by behavioral contract, not convenience.

content.html:
Code Walkthrough › AMyDoor.h
Header excerpt
// MyDoor.h
UCLASS()
class MYPROJECT_API AMyDoor : public AActor
{
    GENERATED_BODY()

private:
    UPROPERTY(VisibleAnywhere, Category = "Door State")
    bool bIsOpen;

    UPROPERTY(EditAnywhere, Category = "Door Settings")
    float DoorOpenDuration;

    UPROPERTY(VisibleAnywhere, Category = "Door State")
    float CurrentOpenAlpha;

public:
    UFUNCTION(BlueprintCallable, Category = "Door Actions")
    void OpenDoor();

    UFUNCTION(BlueprintCallable, Category = "Door Actions")
    void CloseDoor();

    UFUNCTION(BlueprintPure, BlueprintCallable, Category = "Door State")
    bool IsDoorOpen() const;
};
Why these choices
  • bIsOpen: VisibleAnywhere so designers can inspect state but only C++ mutates it.
  • DoorOpenDuration: EditAnywhere so designers tune timing per-instance.
  • Open/Close: BlueprintCallable actions enforce rules when mutating state.
Example scenario
A designer places doors across a level and adjusts DoorOpenDuration per door. Blueprints call OpenDoor; bIsOpen updates internally and designers observe CurrentOpenAlpha in the Details panel during gameplay for debugging.
Misconception
Making DoorOpenDuration both editable and writable from Blueprints is rarely required and risks inconsistent timing changes at runtime.
Check
Does the property need runtime mutation by Blueprints, or is a callable function a better controlled path?

screens.title: MyDoor.cpp — implementation details
screens.narratorSegment: The cpp implementation shows how encapsulation and specifiers work at runtime. The constructor initializes private state: bIsOpen false and CurrentOpenAlpha zero, and sets DoorOpenDuration to a sensible default. BeginPlay can log initial state for debugging. Tick calls UpdateDoorPosition, which interpolates CurrentOpenAlpha toward the target value based on bIsOpen and DoorOpenDuration. The OpenDoor and CloseDoor functions flip bIsOpen and optionally log messages to the screen. IsDoorOpen is a const getter returning bIsOpen. The important point is that the interpolation, logging, and any side effects are centralized inside these functions and UpdateDoorPosition. This centralization enforces invariants: you won't accidentally move CurrentOpenAlpha or flip bIsOpen from another module. A common error is exposing internal helpers publicly or letting Blueprints directly set runtime alpha; that spreads state changes and undermines interpolation logic. The takeaway: keep implementation details internal, expose simple actions and pure queries, and rely on UPROPERTY and UFUNCTION to show or allow access only where appropriate. MyDoor.cpp — implementation details means initialize private state in the constructor, centralize runtime updates in internal methods, and expose actions and pure queries publicly.. In practical terms, constructor, tick, update position, and controlled state changes. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Tick calls UpdateDoorPosition, which interpolates CurrentOpenAlpha toward the target value based on bIsOpen and DoorOpenDuration. The OpenDoor and CloseDoor functions flip bIsOpen and optionally log messages to the screen. IsDoorOpen is a const getter returning bIsOpen. The important point is that the interpolation, logging, and any side effects are centralized inside these functions and UpdateDoorPosition. This centralization enforces invariants: you won't accidentally move CurrentOpenAlpha or flip bIsOpen from another module. A common error is exposing internal helpers publicly or letting Blueprints directly set runtime alpha; that spreads state changes and undermines interpolation logic. The takeaway: keep implementation details internal, expose simple actions and pure queries, and rely on UPROPERTY and UFUNCTION to show or allow access only where appropriate. content.html:
Implementation › MyDoor.cpp
Constructor & Tick
// MyDoor.cpp (excerpt)
AMyDoor::AMyDoor()
{
    PrimaryActorTick.bCanEverTick = true;
    bIsOpen = false;
    DoorOpenDuration = 1.5f;
    CurrentOpenAlpha = 0.0f;
}

void AMyDoor::Tick(float DeltaTime)
{
    Super::Tick(DeltaTime);
    UpdateDoorPosition(DeltaTime);
}
State updates & actions
void AMyDoor::UpdateDoorPosition(float DeltaTime)
{
    float TargetAlpha = bIsOpen ? 1.0f : 0.0f;
    CurrentOpenAlpha = FMath::FInterpTo(CurrentOpenAlpha, TargetAlpha, DeltaTime, 1.0f / DoorOpenDuration);
}

void AMyDoor::OpenDoor()
{
    if (!bIsOpen) bIsOpen = true;
}

bool AMyDoor::IsDoorOpen() const { return bIsOpen; }
Why centralize updates
Single point of truth for interpolation and side effects prevents inconsistent state changes.
Pitfall
Exposing UpdateDoorPosition as public lets other code interfere with interpolation timing.
Takeaway
Keep helpers internal; expose only controlled actions and pure queries.

screens.title: Avoiding over-exposure and fragile APIs
screens.narratorSegment: Teams often rush and mark properties and functions as writable everywhere because it's convenient. The result is a tangled graph of side effects and hard-to-find bugs. Common mistakes include marking internal state as EditAnywhere and BlueprintReadWrite, letting Blueprints set values that should be validated in C++. Another mistake is exposing helper functions that should remain private, which allows external code to bypass invariants. Best practices are straightforward: default to private for fields, provide public BlueprintCallable functions to alter state under controlled rules, and prefer BlueprintReadOnly for properties Blueprints should observe. Use VisibleAnywhere to show runtime state without editing, and use Category tags to help designers find the intended settings. For subclassing, consider protected for necessary extension points but prefer protected accessor methods over raw protected fields. Finally, document the intended ownership: who sets initial values, who mutates them during runtime, and who is allowed to read them. This small discipline dramatically reduces debugging time in collaborative projects. Which of your classes would benefit from converting direct property writes into controlled function calls? Avoiding over-exposure and fragile APIs means default to private, expose actions not fields, prefer read-only blueprint exposure, and document ownership and expected mutators.. fullNarratorScript:
In this chapter you will learn why encapsulation is central to maintainable game code and how C++ access specifiers work together with Unreal Engine's reflection macros to create safe, designer-friendly classes. Encapsulation bundles data and the functions that operate on it, protecting an object's internal state from accidental changes while making clear, stable interfaces for other code and designers. You will see concrete C++ examples that use public, protected, and private to set visibility and then learn how UPROPERTY and UFUNCTION specifiers control editor editability and Blueprint exposure. We'll step through a working AMyDoor actor: how private state is visible but not editable, how editable settings are exposed to designers, and how BlueprintCallable and BlueprintPure functions are chosen. You will also practice common patterns: prefer private state, expose state through controlled functions, and favor read-only exposure to Blueprints unless writing must be allowed. By the end you'll know what to expose, what to protect, and how to keep debugging manageable when teams mix C++ and Blueprints. What small change will make your next actor safer to use in a level?

By the end of this chapter you will understand encapsulation as a protective design pattern, and you will be able to apply C++ access specifiers to enforce it. You will also learn how Unreal's UPROPERTY() specifiers control what designers can edit in the Details panel, and how UFUNCTION() specifiers decide which C++ functions appear in Blueprints as callable or pure nodes. Practically, you'll take a simple AMyDoor actor from private internal state to a designer-friendly component by exposing the right properties for tuning while keeping core state protected in C++. You'll practice declaring private state, exposing edit settings, and adding BlueprintCallable actions that change state only through safe methods. This objective matters because mixing C++ and Blueprints without clear boundaries quickly yields hard-to-debug state changes and accidental behavior. The lesson includes hands-on steps to compile, place an actor, and call functions from Blueprints so you can see editor visibility and Blueprint nodes in action.

These objectives translate directly into team workflows. You will be able to declare private variables to protect core game state while exposing tunable settings to designers through EditAnywhere. You will write BlueprintCallable functions for actions like OpenDoor and CloseDoor so designers can drive behavior without mutating internal state directly. You will choose BlueprintReadOnly for values designers must observe during gameplay, and reserve BlueprintReadWrite only when safe mutation by Blueprints is required. Practically, this reduces accidental state changes that produce hard-to-find bugs in gameplay. The lesson includes a hands-on exercise to create an actor, compile, and verify the Details panel and Blueprint nodes. You will also learn common mistakes to avoid: making everything public or using unchecked Blueprint write access. The goal is a predictable codebase that scales across programmers, designers, and artists.

Encapsulation is an OOP principle that bundles an object's data and the methods that operate on it, while restricting direct external access to those internals. In a game, encapsulation means you expose a clear, small public interface—actions and queries designers or other systems may call—while keeping the actual state and helper functions private. A practical example from this chapter is a door actor: we keep bIsOpen private and provide OpenDoor and CloseDoor functions. That way, any rules about invulnerability frames, locking, or network replication live in the functions, not scattered across Blueprints or other actors. A common misconception is that visibility is only about hiding variables; in practice it is about preserving invariants. If you let every system write to health or position, you lose the ability to enforce game rules consistently. Encapsulation makes refactoring safe: you can change the implementation details—how the door interpolates or what internal timers it uses—without changing its public contract. Your takeaway is simple: expose behavior, not implementation. Ask yourself when adding a variable: does external code really need to set this, or should it call a method that enforces rules?

C++ provides three basic access specifiers: public, protected, and private. Public members form the class's external interface and can be accessed from any code; use them for actions and queries you intend other systems to call. Protected members are available to the class and its subclasses; they are useful when you expect derived classes to extend behavior but do not want general code to modify internals. Private members are accessible only inside the class itself and are the safest place to store core state. A concrete example is a player or door: keep CurrentHealth or bIsOpen private so only controlled functions can mutate them. A typical misconception is treating protected as a free-for-all for subclasses; prefer protected sparingly and provide protected accessors rather than exposing raw fields. When in doubt, default to private and open the minimal interface needed. This discipline helps teams because fixing a rule in one central function propagates everywhere, while scattered writes from various places make reasoning and debugging much harder. Which members in your current class truly need to be public? public, protected, private in C++ means public = external api, protected = for subclasses, private = internal core; default to private and open minimally.. In practical terms, which members should be accessible and to whom. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Unreal's UPROPERTY macro sits on top of C++ access control and tells the Editor and Blueprint system how to surface a member. EditAnywhere makes a property editable in the Details panel for instances and placed actors; use it for tunable settings designers should change at edit time. VisibleAnywhere shows runtime values but prevents editing, which is perfect for showing current internal state without letting designers accidentally overwrite it. BlueprintReadWrite allows Blueprints to both read and set a property, which is convenient but risky for internal state; prefer BlueprintReadOnly when Blueprints only need to observe a value, and use BlueprintCallable functions to mutate state under controlled rules. Category groups properties in the Details panel, improving discoverability for non-programmers. A concrete header example in the chapter shows bIsOpen as VisibleAnywhere and OpenSpeed as EditAnywhere with BlueprintReadWrite. Consider the trade-off: VisibleAnywhere + private C++ access means designers can see a runtime flag but only C++ code can change it. This separation is exactly why UPROPERTY complements C++ encapsulation: one controls code-level visibility, the other controls editor and Blueprint exposure. Which properties in your actors should designers see but never edit during runtime?

UFUNCTION determines how C++ functions appear in Blueprints and how they behave in the graph. BlueprintCallable exposes a function as a standard executable node with execution pins; use it for actions that change state, trigger effects, or perform work. BlueprintPure exposes a function as a read-only node without execution pins; these functions should be const, have no side effects, and return the same output for the same inputs — ideal for getters or deterministic calculations. BlueprintImplementableEvent declares a function that Blueprints implement; the C++ side only declares the contract. BlueprintNativeEvent allows both a C++ implementation and an override in Blueprint, with C++ serving as the fallback. Teams often rush and mark properties and functions as writable everywhere because it's convenient. The result is a tangled graph of side effects and hard-to-find bugs. Common mistakes include marking internal state as EditAnywhere and BlueprintReadWrite, letting Blueprints set values that should be validated in C++. Best practices are straightforward: default to private for fields, provide public BlueprintCallable functions to alter state under controlled rules, and prefer BlueprintReadOnly for properties Blueprints should observe. Here are the compact concepts you should carry forward. First, encapsulation bundles data and methods and prevents scattered state mutation; expose behavior, not raw state. Second, C++ access specifiers control code-level visibility: public for A P I, protected for subclasses, and private for internal invariants. Third, UPROPERTY and UFUNCTION specifiers map C++ members to Editor and Blueprint surfaces. Use EditAnywhere for designer-tunables, VisibleAnywhere to show runtime-only values, BlueprintReadOnly when Blueprints should observe but not write, BlueprintCallable for actions that change state, and BlueprintPure for deterministic, side-effect-free queries.
